title: Time of Entry Becomes the Map

scenes.tts: Bacteria have no meiosis and make no zygote. Yet in 1946, two E coli strains were mixed, and each strain could not make several nutrients. A few cells grew on a plate that supplied none of them. Neither strain alone gave a single colony. So where did the genes come from? How does DNA get from one bacterium into another?
scenes.caption: Bacteria have no meiosis and make no zygote. Yet in 1946, two E. coli strains were mixed, and each strain could not make several nutrients. A few cells grew on a plate that supplied none of them. Neither strain alone gave a single colony. So where did the genes come from? How does DNA get from one bacterium into another?
scenes.visual: Two cells, each with a list of missing abilities, are mixed; green colonies appear on a bare plate; a question mark sits on the gap between the cells where DNA would cross.
scenes.narration: Bacteria have no meiosis and make no zygote. Yet in 1946, two E. coli strains were mixed, and each strain could not make several nutrients. A few cells grew on a plate that supplied none of them. Neither strain alone gave a single colony. So where did the genes come from? How does DNA get from one bacterium into another?

scenes.tts: One route is conjugation. A donor cell touches a recipient and passes DNA straight across. In E coli, the donor carries F, a small circle of DNA. Now and then, F joins the chromosome. That cell is called H F R. Transfer starts inside F, and pulls the chromosome after it in a fixed order.

scenes.visual: A donor with a circular chromosome touches a recipient; a small gold F circle joins the chromosome; markers cross the bridge one after another from the F origin.

scenes.tts: Wollman and Jacob turned that order into a map. They mixed H F R donors with F minus recipients. At set times, they broke the pairs apart in a blender. Then they plated the recipients on medium where only recombinants grow. Each donor gene appeared only in samples taken after a characteristic time.

scenes.visual: Mating pairs are split by a red blender stroke, the recipients move onto a plate; an early plate is empty of colonies for marker a and a later plate has green colonies.

scenes.tts: Take one H F R strain. Marker A first appears at eight minutes. Marker B appears at fourteen, marker C at twenty, and marker D at thirty one. If transfer runs at a steady rate, the time of entry is a position. So the gaps are six, six, and eleven minutes.
scenes.caption: Take one Hfr strain. Marker a first appears at 8 minutes. Marker b appears at 14, marker c at 20, and marker d at 31. If transfer runs at a steady rate, the time of entry is a position. So the gaps are 6, 6, and 11 minutes.
scenes.visual: A minutes axis; markers drop onto it at 8, 14, 20, 31; gap brackets show 6, 6, 11 and a map line is drawn beneath.
scenes.narration: Take one Hfr strain. Marker a first appears at 8 minutes. Marker b appears at 14, marker c at 20, and marker d at 31. If transfer runs at a steady rate, the time of entry is a position. So the gaps are 6, 6, and 11 minutes.

scenes.tts: A second H F R strain gives D at four minutes, C at fifteen, B at twenty one, and A at twenty seven. The order runs backwards, and the times differ. But the gaps are eleven, six, and six. Read in reverse, it is the same map. Its origin lies on the far side of D, so it transfers in the opposite orientation.
scenes.caption: A second Hfr strain gives d at 4 minutes, c at 15, b at 21, and a at 27. The order runs backwards, and the times differ. But the gaps are 11, 6, and 6. Read in reverse, it is the same map. Its origin lies on the far side of d, so it transfers in the opposite orientation.
scenes.visual: Strain two's times are plotted on a second axis in order d c b a; the row flips to match strain one's map; the gaps match; the origin marker sits before d.
scenes.narration: A second Hfr strain gives d at 4 minutes, c at 15, b at 21, and a at 27. The order runs backwards, and the times differ. But the gaps are 11, 6, and 6. Read in reverse, it is the same map. Its origin lies on the far side of d, so it transfers in the opposite orientation.

scenes.tts: H F R strains with F at different sites, in either orientation, gave overlapping orders. Those orders closed into a circle. Jacob and Wollman estimated that the whole chromosome would take about one hundred minutes to enter at a constant rate. That is why the E coli map runs from zero to one hundred minutes. Keep this rule: the gaps are the map.
